title: RAG systems: project 1
why: RAG appears in roughly two-thirds of applied LLM listings. This is the project you'll be asked about first, so it has to work, cite and refuse properly.
outcomes: Build an ingestion pipeline: parse, clean, chunk, embed, store
Retrieve with vector, keyword and hybrid search, then rerank
Generate grounded answers with inline citations
Refuse cleanly when the documents don't hold the answer
lessons: Pick a real corpus of 50 or more public documents (DfE guidance, exam specifications, Ofsted frameworks)
Ingestion: parse PDFs and HTML, clean, chunk, store in pgvector with metadata
Retrieval: top-k vector search, then add keyword search for hybrid
Add a reranker and compare results on 20 questions
Generation: grounded prompt with inline citations and an explicit refusal path
Ship it: FastAPI plus a thin web page, deployed, README with design decisions
resources: IBM RAG and Agentic AI Professional Certificate
Take the RAG courses now, agent courses later
method: Build the simplest pipeline first without a framework, around 150 lines. Then bring in a framework only where it saves you code. You'll know what it's doing for you, which interviewers test.
build: Project 1: a deployed RAG app over your corpus that cites its sources and says 'not in the documents' when it should.

proj.about: A question-answering app over a set of documents you choose, such as policies, specifications or guidance. It finds the right passages, answers with citations and says plainly when the documents don't hold the answer.
skills: Refusal when the answer isn't there
proj.market: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and vector databases appear in most applied LLM job adverts. It's the project interviewers ask about first.

worked.t: Mini RAG: ask three policy pages
worked.intro: A complete, tiny version of project 1 in about 80 lines. Build it in an evening, then grow it into your own project with a real corpus, Postgres and a deploy.

steps.md:
```bash
uv init mini-rag && cd mini-rag
uv add anthropic numpy python-dotenv
```

Put `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in `.env`. For embeddings this example uses a tiny bag-of-words vector so it runs anywhere; you'll swap in a real embeddings API in step 5.

```py
DOCS = {
    "leave-p3": "Staff may carry over up to five days of annual leave into the next year.",
    "leave-p4": "Carried-over leave must be used by 31 March or it is lost.",
    "expenses-p2": "Expenses over £50 need a receipt and line manager approval.",
}
```

Three short passages with ids you can cite. Your project will have hundreds.

```py
import anthropic
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def answer(question, threshold=0.15):
    hits = [h for h in retrieve(question) if h[1] >= threshold]
    if not hits:
        return "I can't find that in the documents."
    sources = "\n".join(f"[{d}] {DOCS[d]}" for d, _ in hits)
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5", max_tokens=200,
        system="Answer only from the sources. Cite like [leave-p3]. If they don't answer it, say you can't find it.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"<sources>\n{sources}\n</sources>\n\nQuestion: {question}"}])
    return msg.content[0].text

print(answer("When do I have to use carried-over leave?"))
print(answer("What is the canteen menu?"))
```

The second question should be refused before the model is even called. Check your provider's model list for current names.

- Swap `vec` for a real embeddings API and store vectors in Postgres with pgvector.
- Add keyword search and merge with reciprocal rank fusion.
- Check that every citation in the answer is one you sent.
- Wrap `answer` in a FastAPI `POST /ask`, containerise it and deploy.
- Write ten real questions and record how many retrieve the right source. That table goes in your README.
